item.title: Brief #31: What China’s new AI export controls really mean (spoiler: not the end of open weight)
item.description: Also: Kimi curbs cyber offense; AI’s employment impact
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Wagner
item.content:encoded:
In this issue, we focus on one big topic: the intricacies of China’s proposed AI export controls. We close with a few other notable developments, including how Moonshot AI filters cyber offense data, and how the government aims to address AI-driven unemployment.

What happened: China has proposed rules that would give the government a say over whether certain AI technologies can be exported. A draft revision of the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export released by the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) on October 16 would add 40 items to the Catalogue, of which 23 are AI-related, covering certain large language models, agents, chip designs, compute clusters and offensive cyber tooling (the remaining 17 items relate to biomedicine and photovoltaics).

item.title: Brief #30: What’s next for China–US AI talks after the Xi–Trump summit
item.description: Also: expert draft AI Laws; Bytedance’s new safety department; how DeepSeek mitigates agentic reward hacking; AI safety funding
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Wagner
item.content:encoded:
Last month, Xi and Trump agreed to continued China–US AI dialogue, with the two sides meeting again in November, plus a bilateral channel for AI incidents.

Chinese state media suggest the coming round of talks in November should flesh out the incident channel, align risk definitions, and start with worst-case risks.

Two new unofficial AI Law drafts join a crowded field of expert proposals, but a national AI Law remains uncertain.

ByteDance upgraded its Responsible AI team to a new Alignment & Preparedness Department focused on frontier risks.

Also: we are hiring! More details at the very end.

What happened: One day after our last newsletter, President Xi met President Trump in the US on September 24-25.

item.title: 10 Key Insights from Concordia AI’s “Frontier AI Risk Monitoring Platform”
item.description: Concordia AI has launched the Frontier AI Risk Monitoring Platform, along with our inaugural 2025 Q3 Monitoring Report. It tracks models from 15 leading developers worldwide for risks in four domains: cyber offense, biological risks, chemical risks, and loss-of-control, making it the first such platform in China focused on catastrophic risks.
item.content:encoded:
Concordia AI has launched the Frontier AI Risk Monitoring Platform, along with our inaugural 2025 Q3 Monitoring Report. It tracks models from 15 leading developers worldwide for risks in four domains: cyber offense, biological risks, chemical risks, and loss-of-control, making it the first such platform in China focused on catastrophic risks.

You can find more detail, including our methodology, on the interactive platform. The South China Morning Post (SCMP) has also covered the launch in an exclusive story.

As AI capabilities accelerate, we lack insight on some critical questions:

What are the key trends and drivers for frontier AI risks?

Are these risks increasing or decreasing?

Where are the safety gaps most severe?
